verdicts.strongest_argument: Both facts are correct and both were traded in DELL, by name, on the day. Super Micro's margin shock was NOT new on 11 Aug: SMCI pre-announced it on 21 Jul 2026 in an 8-K business update giving 15-17% gross margin against 8.2-8.4% guidance -- six weeks before the print the hunter cites, so the 11 Aug 17.5% was the confirmation of an already-disclosed number, not the disclosure. Lenovo's ISG print landed 13 Aug and DELL rose ~4% pre-market on it and made its 52-week high that session, with the read-across stated in the headline of the wire copy ('Dell Stock Gains as Super Micro, Lenovo Beat Expectations', Benzinga 13 Aug; 'Super Micro, Dell, and HP Jump After Strong Lenovo Earnings', 24/7 Wall St 13 Aug). That is the 70-85 anchor almost exactly: in the wire copy, and visibly in the price on the date it became known. The finding also agrees with the one thing the baseline measures cleanly -- a 25-delta skew of -9.3 vol points, upside paid, on a two-sided chain with a 3.3%-of-mid ATM spread. A bullish claim that agrees with the measured lean of the option market is agreement, not information. The steelman for the hunter is that DELL has since given the move back (-10.8% from the 52w high, -5.6% over 20 days), so the read-across is no longer in the price. I reject that reading of the tape: the give-back has identifiable, dated, Dell-specific causes -- a Morgan Stanley downgrade explicitly on memory chip costs, the 'memory boom splits the AI hardware trade' rotation (DELL -6%, WDC +5%), Aug 18 -3.3%, Aug 28 -3.7% after HP Inc's results -- i.e. the market absorbed the bull read-across and was then handed better evidence. A price falling on subsequent information does not un-price the prior information. Where I concede ground: the *quantified* size of the Lenovo beat (9.1% ISG operating margin against a ~4.6% sell-side average, sourced off UBS 4.0% / CLSA 5.2% / JPM 4.8% / MS 4.5%) is only laid out in an obscure outlet (BigGo Finance), not in Western wire copy, and that specific arithmetic is the genuinely under-drawn part. Separately, the hunter's mechanism is weaker than stated: SMCI's own filing attributes the margin upside 'primarily to a favorable customer and product mix', not to passing component-cost inflation through. So I accept the facts, accept the sign, and reject the novelty and part of the mechanism.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Super Micro pre-announced Q4 FY2026 gross margin of 15-17% versus guidance of 8.2-8.4%, attributed 'primarily to a favorable customer and product mix' -- six weeks before the 11 Aug print the finding rests on.
Wire headline explicitly making the Super Micro / Lenovo beat the reason DELL shares were gaining.
DELL up ~4% pre-market on strong Lenovo earnings, alongside SMCI and HP.
Lenovo ISG operating margin 9.1% versus UBS 4.0%, CLSA 5.2%, JPMorgan 4.8%, Morgan Stanley 4.5% -- nearly double consensus.
Final Q4 FY2026 gross margin 17.5% versus 9.9% in Q3'26 and 9.5% in Q4'25.

The preview coverage the finding cites for framing; states Dell's COO has said the company adjusts prices frequently and that Dell's own guidance assumes the repricing keeps working -- i.e. the pass-through case is already the company's published position.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Skew of -9.3 vol points (upside paid) with put/call OI at 1.12 says the option market is already leaning the way this finding leans, on the day's best-measured chain (ATM spread 3.3% of mid). The 52-week high in the baseline (-10.78% from spot, so a ~494.5 close) is dated 13 Aug -- the exact session the read-across became known -- which is the price record of it being priced. The 20-day run-up of -5.58% is the give-back, and it is attributable to dated, named, Dell-specific bear catalysts (Morgan Stanley memory downgrade, HP Inc results 26-27 Aug) rather than to the read-across being forgotten.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Evidence that DELL's 13 Aug move was driven by Lenovo's $54bn AI backlog alone with no analyst marking-up of Dell's ISG *margin* line, plus a current sell-side ISG operating-margin bar still sitting near 11% -- which would leave the margin leg genuinely un-modelled even though the news was headline.
verdicts.notes_on_correctness: Facts accepted as stated; Super Micro 17.5% GAAP vs 8.2-8.4% prior guidance and Lenovo ISG 9.1% vs ~4.6% consensus both verify. Objection is to novelty (SMCI pre-announced 21 Jul; Lenovo traded in DELL 13 Aug) and to the stated mechanism (SMCI attributes its beat to mix, not cost pass-through).

verdicts.strongest_argument: This is the highest-priced of the two and the one where I also reject the sign. Every number in it was published on IDC's release day and syndicated across dozens of outlets in the week of 8-14 July 2026 -- 68.2m units, -4.9%, Dell 9.3m and -5%, share 'practically stable at 13.6 percent', and the revenue-up-on-units-down dynamic phrased as 'vendors' revenues are rising because price increases are being implemented faster than demand is falling'. That last clause is not a buried implication the hunter drew out; it is the headline of the hunter's own cited source (PC Gamer) and it is in the body of Igor's Lab on 13 Jul, 9to5Mac on 8 Jul, Asymco on 14 Jul and Electronics Weekly. When the finding's conclusion is the title of the article the finding cites, priced_in is near the top of the range. Two further objections. First, size: the '20-40% year over year' comparable-line price figure does not reconcile with the sources -- IDC's own PCD forecast is ASPs +18.3% for 2026, Igor's Lab cites Gartner at +17% average PC prices, and the vendor list-price warnings reported for H2 2026 are 15-20%. I accept the direction of pricing power and reject the magnitude as roughly double what the record supports. Second, and more seriously, the sign: the closest and freshest comparable points the other way and has already been traded in DELL. HP Inc reported fiscal Q3 on 26-27 Aug 2026 for a quarter ended 31 July -- a three-of-three-month overlap with Dell's fiscal Q2, against IDC's two-of-three -- and Personal Systems operating margin came in at 4.6%, DOWN from 5.4%, with the company stating that higher commodity costs 'more than offset repricing and cost reductions', PC units -16%, and no margin recovery expected until fiscal 2027. That is a direct, same-window, same-product refutation of 'pricing-power event rather than a margin event for OEMs', it is eight weeks newer than the IDC data, and DELL fell 3.7% on 28 Aug in its wake. So the market has not merely seen this finding; it has seen it, then seen it superseded. Finally, the mechanism is small even if right: CSG is roughly a quarter to a third of the ~$45bn consensus revenue line for this print and much less of operating income, and the AI server line is what a 9.29% implied move is being paid for. A 100bp CSG margin swing is not a 9% stock.

prior_publication.what_it_says: 68.2m units -4.9%, Dell 9.3m and -5% with share stable at 13.6%, and 'vendors' revenues are rising because price increases are being implemented faster than demand is falling'; cites Gartner at ~+17% average PC prices, not 20-40%.
IDC Q2 2026 preliminary PC tracker published, Apple up, broader market down.
Independent cross-check of the same IDC -4.9% Q2 2026 figure against Omdia.
Q2 PC shipments down 4.9% as memory stays short.

HP fiscal Q3 (quarter ended 31 July, full overlap with Dell FQ2): Personal Systems operating margin 4.6% versus 5.4% a year earlier because higher commodity costs more than offset repricing; PC units -16%; no margin recovery until FY2027.
HP down 5% specifically because memory costs pressured PC margins -- the same-quarter counterexample to the pricing-power-not-margin thesis.
IDC's own PCD outlook has PC ASPs rising 18.3% in 2026, against the finding's claimed 20-40% comparable-line increases.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Nothing in the tape marks 8-14 July as a DELL event; the run-up windows in the baseline (5d -2.28%, 20d -5.58%) start well after it, so this information has had eight weeks and two subsequent PC-sector prints to be absorbed. The dated moves that ARE in the 20-day window (-3.3% on 18 Aug, -3.7% on 28 Aug) both run against this finding's sign. The -9.3 skew still leans up, so the residual bull case is bid, not free.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A Dell-specific disclosure that CSG gross margin *rate* expanded year over year in the May-July quarter, or evidence that consensus CSG operating margin for this print was cut to HP-like levels after 27 Aug and therefore now sits below what the IDC pricing data implies.

interactions: Substantially one mechanism counted twice, though not entirely. Both findings assert the same proposition -- assemblers are passing component-cost inflation through rather than absorbing it -- both lean positive, both agree with the baseline's measured -9.3 skew, and both draw on the same mid-August/July news cycle that DELL has already traded. If DELL#0 is right, DELL#1 adds close to nothing to the position, so they should not be summed. Where they genuinely differ is segment and evidence quality: DELL#0 is about ISG servers and rests on two live comparables in the same quarter; DELL#1 is about CSG PCs and rests on IDC unit/price data that a closer comparable (HP Inc, 26-27 Aug, identical quarter end) contradicts on the exact point at issue. That asymmetry is the useful part -- the server leg of the thesis survives with a novelty problem, the PC leg has a sign problem. They also share a documentary dependency I judged against both: the 13 Aug wire copy that named the Super Micro / Lenovo read-across as the reason DELL was up, which is simultaneously the best evidence the mechanism is real and the best evidence it is already in the price. Finally, DELL#0's own citation of Dell 'preview coverage' points at the Motley Fool 31 Aug piece, which I read: it states Dell's COO's position that the company reprices frequently and that guidance assumes repricing keeps working -- so the pass-through case is the company's published position, not a contrarian one.
